GSM8K: 36 iterations without rationalization plus 10 with it (Section 4.5); CQA: run to saturation, number of iterations not reported|not reported|fully reversible|self-improvement|in-task|CQA dev 72.5% (GPT-J fine-tuned directly 60.0%, few-shot CoT 36.6%, fine-tuned GPT-3 30x larger 73.0%, Table 1); GSM8K 10.7% (direct fine-tuning 5.8%, Table 2); arithmetic 89.5% after 16 iterations (no-rationale baseline 76.3%, Section 4.3)|Without rationalization the loop stalls and cannot solve new problems in the training set (Sections 1 and 3.2); needs few-shot performance above chance, and GPT-2 cannot bootstrap even on arithmetic; tasks with a high chance of guessing right (e.g. binary choice) admit many poor rationales (Section 6); raising the sampling temperature degrades rationales into meaningless scratchpads (Section 5); without the few-shot prompt the style drifts and rationalization gets worse over training (Section 5); with hints present during training the model learns to copy the hinted answer (Appendix A.6); can amplify dataset biases, and faithfulness of the rationales is not guaranteed (Appendix G); training becomes unstable after new digit lengths are added (Section 4.3)|full text|medium|Feedback details: automated evaluation, rationales filtered against the ground-truth answer (Section 3.1: “filter the generated rationales to include only the ones which result in the correct answer”); rationalization gives the ground-truth answer as a hint but still filters on whether the answer matches (Algorithm 1, line 6). Loop: humans only write the initial few-shot prompts (10 for CQA, edited by hand by the authors, Section 4.1). Evidence: CQA dev, GSM8K test and arithmetic are all held-out sets of the same tasks; 9- to 10-digit addition is length extrapolation and still counts as in-task (Section 4.3). Human evaluation (20 Prolific crowdworkers) only rates rationale quality and is not part of the loop (Section 4.4). Verification cost: only a single TPU-v3 node is mentioned, with no running time reported (Appendix H). MGSM 53.4% (LLM Debate 39.0%); ARC 13.7% (COT-SC 8.0%, GPT-3.5); the agent found on MGSM transfers to GSM8K at 69.5% (best baseline 43.6%) (Tables 1-3)|Evaluated only on one-step question-answering tasks (Section 6); optimizes a single objective (performance); the evaluation function looks only at a numeric score, which is costly and loses information (Section 6, Appendix J); gains are small in the science and multi-task domains, which the authors attribute to the base model lacking knowledge (Section 4.2); agents found in the math domain do worse in other domains than agents searched for those domains, and only match the baselines in the science domain (Appendix A, Table 5); the best agent on GPT-3.5 is no longer the best when moved to stronger models (Section 6); in the math domain, starting from an empty archive works better, for reasons not investigated (Appendix I); all datasets are sampled subsets (Appendices D and E)|partial text|medium|Feedback details: automated evaluation; each new agent's accuracy or F1 on the target domain's validation set is written into the archive for the meta agent to consult in the next iteration (Section 3: “we calculate the performance ... as the metrics for the meta agent to maximize”); every new agent is added to the archive and none is removed (Appendix H, Algorithm 1, line 12). The meta agent also runs two rounds of self-reflection to check novelty and self-corrects up to 5 times on errors; these do not decide what is kept. Loop: people only write the framework code, the domain descriptions and the initial seed agents (Section 3, Appendix B); Section 6 mentions “thorough manual inspections” of the generated code as a safety measure, and the paper does not say whether this is inside the loop. Evidence: Tables 2, 4 and 5 transfer to math and non-math benchmarks not used in the search, and Table 3 transfers to other base models; all evaluations were run by the authors. Verification cost: Appendix J reports only the API cost per run (about USD 500 for ARC, about USD 300 for the other domains), not the time. Publication status: the first page of the PDF reads “Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025”.
